participants: Andrew Jin / Andrew Musial (Primal Instinct) — closer
Referenced but not present: Manny Núñez (prospect from the previous day), Kim Forbes-Sobers (setter), Trevor (programme owner)
summary: Thirty-three minute manager one-to-one between sales manager Chris Klevan and closer Andrew Musial, the day after the Manny Núñez call. Chris opened with Andrew's month-to-date call-to-close rate of 33.3% against a 25% KPI and told him he is a good closer with two fixable problems: an unengaging pitch, and jumping on every objection without first isolating whether it is the real one. The bulk of the call was a detailed walkthrough of when a money objection is genuine capacity versus fear, including how to size a payment plan against a prospect's monthly surplus so it leaves headroom, and when to deploy the three-month option, a two-pay, and 'love it or leave it'. Chris used the Manny call as the worked example and diagnosed it correctly — that Manny simply needed payment logistics and did not need his commitment challenged. He also coached Andrew not to interrupt prospects mid-disclosure, citing a specific moment where Andrew cut Manny off just as he was opening up about pain at 38. The last third covered operational questions: how to log dispositions in the Close CRM, how to handle a prospect lost to a double-booking mishap, and why every call slot is deliberately double-booked.
notable: CLOSE RATE BENCHMARK — 'Your call to close is about 33.3%, so pretty good... The KPI is 25%. You're doing well.' This is the internal target any close-rate computed from this corpus should be read against.

CRM DISPOSITION RULE — this materially changes how any CRM-derived close rate should be read. Chris: 'lost is only for if somebody is like, dude, I'm not working with your company. Or they've already bought another program, or they straight up tell you no, basically... if it's still like, I want to do it, but it's like X, Y, Z thing, and I need to wait X amount of time to do it, then it's follow-up.' Under this rule almost every non-close is logged as a follow-up, so the CRM 'lost' count is not a loss count.

OFF-MENU TIERS ARE OFFICIAL — the three-month option, a 'two-pay', and 'love it or leave it' were all discussed as established tools with manager-defined deployment rules. Andrew asked 'When is the moment that we should present the three-month option?' and Chris answered 'If you find out they only have enough money to do the three-month option.' None of these appear in the stated $6,000/6mo and $9,000/12mo offer.

FINANCED PRICE IS $7,200 — Andrew, describing a scenario: 'we present the financing options, but that scares them too, because it's $7,200. So that's too much.' A financed six-month deal therefore costs the prospect $7,200 against a $6,000 cash price. No prospect in this batch was told a financed total; they were told only that interest 'is not high, but it's different depending on your credit score.'

PAYMENT PLANS ARE STANDARD AND MANAGER-SIZED — Chris: 'I usually always pitch a payment plan that is right around. If somebody has $1,000 left over at the end of each month, I would probably try to finance them and try to see if I can get them in on payment for the $650 or whatever.' This directly contradicts reps telling prospects that set payment plans do not exist.

DOUBLE BOOKING IS DELIBERATE POLICY — Chris: 'the reason the double booking is there is because historically the show rates weren't that great, so we couldn't reliably say that if we just had one person in the slot that they would for sure show. And so what we do is if we put two people in the slot, there is a much higher chance that you will end with one call at least.' Every closer slot holds two prospects by design.

A PROSPECT WAS LOST TO THE DOUBLE BOOKING — Andrew reported a prospect who received repeated confirmation messages, was called ten minutes after his slot, was rescheduled, and then cancelled: 'he sent me a message that he got so many messages reconfirming and so on... So he didn't feel good about it. And he doesn't want to move forward with us.' Chris coached an apology script leaving the door open.

MANAGER READ ON MANNY — Chris independently assessed Manny as unaffordable: 'Listen to this guy's situation. He's got two mortgages. He's paying this. He's doing this. He's got maybe $500 left over at the end of each month. Like, this isn't a priority thing. He's spread thin.' He nonetheless directed the follow-up toward financing: 'you're just gonna have to figure out a payment plan with him and see if you can make it work, finance it or something.' He also predicted the no-show: 'Is Manny gonna show? I don't think so.'

POSITIVE COACHING — several genuinely protective instructions. 'When they tell you it's straight up finances, just believe them until you have a reason not to.' 'Last thing I want to do is put you in a tight spot financially.' On sizing plans, an explicit warning against leaving a prospect with no savings buffer. And a strong correction on interrupting: 'that guy was just about to let loose a very emotional thing and open up to you, and you cut him off to ask him how bad the pain is. Instead of just being like, damn, man, that's frustrating. Tell me more about that.'

CREDIT CARD ADVICE — Chris on a prospect saving $3,000 a month with a $15,000 credit card: 'can I tell you what I would do if I were you? Dude, would pay it in full and put it on the credit card.' The transcript is ambiguous as to whether $15,000 is the balance or the available limit, so it is recorded here rather than flagged.

Chris confirmed the correct handling of Manny was structural, not psychological: 'there was no real need to challenge his commitment level of doing it, like he wanted to do the program, and you could see it.'
